questions.concept: Monocot vs dicot — the reliable characters
questions.question: Why is leaf vein pattern a more reliable monocot/dicot indicator than leaf size?
questions.solution: Venation reflects deep anatomy: monocots have PARALLEL veins (their vascular bundles are scattered in the stem, matching the leaf), dicots RETICULATE (a network matching the ring-arranged vascular bundles). Size is variable with environment; venation is fixed by the group's developmental plan. Structural, developmentally-linked characters are the reliable ones.

questions.question: Why does every organism carry a two-part Latin name (e.g. Mangifera indica), and what does each part do?
questions.solution: The binomial gives every species ONE universally accepted name, ending the chaos of regional common names. Genus (capitalised) groups related species; species epithet (lowercase) pinpoints the organism; together they are unique. Written italicised/underlined — the format itself signals 'a species name'.

questions.question: Why are bryophytes called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' while pteridophytes broke free of that limit? Name the key innovation.
questions.solution: Bryophytes lack vascular tissue and need water for sperm to swim to the egg — they live in damp places and stay small (the 'amphibian' analogy). Pteridophytes evolved VASCULAR TISSUE (xylem/phloem), letting them grow tall and transport water internally; fertilisation still needs water, but the plant body is independent. Vascular tissue is the innovation that lifted the size ceiling.

questions.question: What does the word 'gymnosperm' literally mean, and how does the angiosperm's ovary change the seed's fate?
questions.solution: Gymnosperm = 'naked seed': ovules sit exposed on scales (cone), no ovary, so seeds are uncovered. Angiosperms enclose ovules in an OVARY that becomes the fruit — protecting the seed and recruiting animals for dispersal. Enclosure + fruit is the angiosperm's dual advantage.

questions.question: In plants, why does a haploid gametophyte alternate with a diploid sporophyte — what does each generation contribute?
questions.solution: The gametophyte (n) produces gametes by MITOSIS; fusion restores 2n; the sporophyte (2n) produces spores by MEIOSIS, restarting the cycle. The alternation lets the life cycle both reshuffle genes (meiosis) and multiply without fertilisation (spores) — genetic mixing and dispersal in one lifecycle.
